summary: Defines MIB modules for managing Ethernet in the First Mile Copper interfaces, 10PASS-TS and 2BASE-TL, as specified by IEEE 802.3ah. They extend the existing Ethernet-like interfaces and MAU MIB modules with objects for these copper links. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5066 adds management objects for copper lines running Ethernet, so that the same network management tools used everywhere else can see and control them. It covers both the whole port and each individual line, and it adds tables that say which lines could be joined together.

questions: what is a pme in efm
subtitle: How a network manager sees a copper pair that has been turned into an Ethernet link.

tldr.problem: Copper telephone lines can be turned into Ethernet links, but a manager needs to see them, configure them and tell a healthy line from a broken one in the same way it sees any other interface.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two MIB modules. One adds objects for the new interfaces and for the individual copper pairs under them, and the other adds two tables that describe which of those layers could be connected to which.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from November 2007 and was later updated by RFC 7124. It warns that writing to the objects can disrupt a live link, so management access needs protecting.

today: RFC 5066 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2007. It was later updated by RFC 7124; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What This MIB Adds
sections.content:
This document defines Management Information Base modules for use with network management protocols in TCP/IP-based internets. It describes extensions to the Ethernet-like Interfaces MIB and the Medium Attachment Unit MIB with a set of objects for managing Ethernet in the First Mile Copper interfaces 10PASS-TS and 2BASE-TL, defined in IEEE Std 802.3ah-2004, which has since been integrated into IEEE Std 802.3-2005. In addition, a set of objects is defined describing the cross-connect capability of a managed device with multi-layer, or stacked, interfaces, extending the stack management objects in the Interfaces Group MIB and the Inverted Stack Table MIB modules.

New Ethernet-like interfaces have been defined in IEEE Standard 802.3ah-2004, also known as Ethernet in the First Mile. In particular, the 2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS physical interfaces, defined over voice-grade copper pairs, have been specified for the long and short reach respectively. These interfaces, collectively called EFM Copper, are based on Single-pair High-speed Digital Subscriber Line and Very High speed Digital Subscriber Line technology, supporting optional Physical Medium Entity aggregation, also known as multi-pair bonding, with variable rates.

The 2BASE-TL PHY is capable of providing at least 2 Mbps over a 2700 m long single copper pair with a mean Bit Error Rate of 10^-7, using a 5 dB target noise margin. The 10PASS-TS PHY is capable of providing at least 10 Mbps over a 750 m long single copper pair with a mean Bit Error Rate of 10^-7, using a 6 dB target noise margin. Managed objects for the Operation, Administration and Maintenance and the Ethernet over Passive Optical Networks clauses of IEEE 802.3ah are defined in the EFM-COMMON-MIB and the EFM-EPON-MIB respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: Telephone wire can carry Ethernet. This document gives the network manager the same kind of view of that wire that it already has of a network card in a server.

sections.title: The Internet-Standard Management Framework
sections.content:
Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base or MIB. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol, and objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the Structure of Management Information. This memo specifies MIB modules that are compliant to SMIv2, which is described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The two MIB modules defined here extend five existing ones: the Interfaces Group MIB, the Ethernet-Like MIB, the MAU MIB, the SHDSL MIB and the VDSL MIB. The 2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS PHYs specified in the EFM-CU-MIB module are stacked, also called aggregated or bonded, Ethernet interfaces, and as such are managed using the generic interface management objects defined in the IF-MIB. The stack management, that is, the actual connection of the sub-layers to the top-layer interface, is done via the ifStackTable and its inverse ifInvStackTable. The new tables ifCapStackTable and its inverse ifInvCapStackTable, defined in the IF-CAP-STACK-MIB module, extend the stack management with an ability to describe possible connections, or cross-connect capability, when a flexible cross-connect matrix is present between the interface layers.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is the list of things a device lets a manager read and change over SNMP. This one adds entries to the standard lists rather than starting from scratch, so old management software still understands the basics.

sections.title: How a Copper Port Is Built from Layers
sections.content:
An EFMCu interface can aggregate up to 32 Physical Medium Entity sub-layer devices, modems, using the PME Aggregation Function. A generic EFMCu device can have a number of Physical Coding Sublayer ports, each connected to a Media Access Controller via a Medium Independent Interface at the upper layer, and cross-connected to a number of underlying PMEs, with a single PCS per PME relationship.

Each PME in the aggregated EFMCu port is represented in the Interface table as a separate interface, with ifType of shdsl(169) for 2BASE-TL or vdsl(97) for 10PASS-TS. The ifSpeed for each PME SHALL return the actual data bitrate of the active PME, for example for 2BASE-TL PMEs a multiple of 64 Kbps, and a zero value SHALL be returned when the PME is initializing or down. The ifSpeed of the PCS is the sum of the current operating data rates of all PMEs in the aggregation group, without the 64/65-octet encapsulation overhead and PAF overhead, but accounting for the Inter-Frame Gaps.

Layered above the PMEs, the port is presented as an ordinary Ethernet interface: the ifEntry represents a consolidation of the LLC, MAC and PCS sub-layers, with ifType ethernetCsmacd(6) and an ifMauEntry whose ifMauType is dot3MauType2BaseTL or dot3MauType10PassTS. The implementation of the EtherLike-MIB and the MAU-MIB is REQUIRED for EFMCu interfaces, and two new ifMauType values were defined for them. The interpretation of the ifMauMediaAvailable values also differs because of the aggregation: unknown means the interface is initializing, ready means it is down but at least one PME is ready for handshake, available means it is up with all PMEs up, notAvailable means it is down with all PMEs down, availableReduced means it is up with a link fault at the receive direction in one or more PMEs but at least one PME up, and pmdLinkFault means a link fault at the receive direction in all PMEs.
sections.plainLanguage: One copper port is really a stack: a set of individual lines at the bottom, and one Ethernet interface on top that borrows their combined speed. The MIB exposes both levels separately.

sections.title: Discovery and PME Assignment
sections.content:
The EFMCu ports may optionally support a discovery operation, whereby PMEs, during initialization, exchange information about their respective aggregation groups. This information can then be used to detect copper misconnections, or for an automatic assignment of the local PMEs into aggregation groups instead of a fixed pre-configuration. The MIB modules allow a network management application to control the EFM Discovery mechanism and query its results, and the mechanism can work only if PAF is supported and enabled.

The RFC gives pseudo-code for discovery and automatic PME assignment on a PAF-enabled multi-PCS device at a central office. For each PCS port that is PAF enabled and has room for more PMEs, the manager assigns a unique 6-octet local discovery code, for example the MAC address, and then goes over all disconnected PMEs that could possibly be connected to that PCS, as listed in ifCapStackTable but not in ifStackTable. It writes the local code to the remote discovery code register of a candidate PME with an atomic Set-if-Clear action, which succeeds only if the remote register was zero, and then reads it back. If the value matches the local code and there is still room in the aggregation group, the PME is added to the PCS and the count of PMEs is incremented; the remaining PMEs at the same remote device are then connected too.

An SNMP agent for an EFMCu device builds the ifCapStackTable and its inverse from the information in the Clause 45 PME_Available_register, and adding a PME to the ifStackTable row for a specific PCS involves the actual connection of the PME to the PCS, done by modifying the Clause 45 PME_Aggregate_register. The PCS port does not have to be operationally down for the connection to succeed, and a dynamic PME addition and removal may be implemented with an available PME being initialized first by setting its ifAdminStatus to up and then added to an operationally up PCS port. It is RECOMMENDED that removal of the last operationally up PME from an operationally up PCS be rejected, as this would completely drop the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of being told which lines to group, the manager can ask the far end to identify itself. Each side writes a code into the other and reads it back; a matching code means the two are on the same bundle and can be grouped.

sections.title: Bringing a Port Up and Reading Its State
sections.content:
EFMCu ports built on xDSL technology require a lengthy initialization or training process before any data can pass. During this initialization both ends of a link work cooperatively to achieve the required data rate on a particular copper pair, and sometimes, when the copper line is too long or the noise too high, the training process may fail to achieve a specific target rate with the required characteristics.

The ifAdminStatus object from the IF-MIB controls the desired state of a PCS with all the PMEs connected to it, or of an individual PME port. Setting it to up instructs the PCS or PME to start the initialization process, which may take tens of seconds for EFMCu ports, especially if PAF is involved. The ifOperStatus object shows the operational state of an interface, extended by the ifMauMediaAvailable object for the PCS and by efmCuPmeOperStatus for the PME interfaces. A disconnected PME may be initialized by changing ifAdminStatus from down to up, and changing it to up on the PCS initializes all PMEs connected to that PCS. In the case of PAF some interfaces may fail to initialize while others succeed. The PCS is considered operationally up if at least one PME aggregated by its PAF is operationally up; it SHALL be considered operationally lowerLayerDown when all PMEs connected to it are down, and operationally notPresent if it is not connected to any PME. The PCS or PME interface SHALL remain operationally down during initialization.

The efmCuPmeOperStatus object expands the PME's ifOperStatus value of down into three more specific values: downNotReady, meaning the link is down and the PME does not detect handshake tones from its peer; downReady, meaning the link is down but the PME has detected them; and init, meaning the PME is initializing. The capacity of the local aggregation function is reported by efmCuPAFCapacity, whose syntax is Unsigned32 (1..32) and which gives the number of PMEs that can be aggregated by the local PAF, while efmCuNumPMEs, with the syntax Unsigned32 (0..32), gives the number currently assigned.
sections.plainLanguage: Turning on a copper port is slow, because both ends have to work out together what the line can carry. The MIB reports that separately: whether a line is up, down but waiting, down because the far end is silent, or still initializing.

sections.title: The Two MIB Modules and Their Tables
sections.content:
The main management objects defined in the EFM-CU-MIB module are split into two groups: efmCuPort, containing objects for configuration, capabilities, status and notifications common to all EFMCu PHYs, and efmCuPme, containing objects for configuration, capabilities, status and notifications of EFMCu PMEs. The efmCuPme group in turn contains efmCuPme2B and efmCuPme10P groups, which define PME profiles specific to 2BASE-TL and 10PASS-TS PMEs, as well as PME-specific status information. The IF-CAP-STACK-MIB module contains two tables: ifCapStackTable, holding objects that define possible relationships among the sub-layers of an interface with flexible cross-connect, and ifInvCapStackTable, an inverse of it.

The ifCapStackTable is modelled on ifStackTable but is read-only, because it reflects device capability rather than what is actually connected. It says which sub-layers may possibly run on top of which other sub-layers. For example, when the sub-layer with ifIndex value x can be connected to run on top of the sub-layer with ifIndex value y, the table contains ifCapStackStatus.x.y set to true, and the row does not exist if the connection is impossible. The inverse table has the ifIndex values in its INDEX clause in the reverse order, lower-layer interface first, which gives an efficient way to read a subset of the forward table.

Because a managed node can have a large number of EFMCu PHYs, and most PMEs are provisioned identically, the module makes use of configuration profiles. A profile is a set of parameters used either for configuration or representation of a PME, and the same profile can be shared by multiple PME ports. The profiles are defined in the efmCuPme2BProfileTable and efmCuPme10PProfileTable. There are 12 predefined standard profiles for 2BASE-TL and 22 standard profiles for 10PASS-TS, defined in 802.3ah and dedicated for rapid provisioning, and the EFM-CU-MIB defines two additional predefined profiles for best-effort provisioning of 2BASE-TL PMEs. A specific profile is assigned to a PME through the efmCuPmeAdminProfile object; if that is zero, the efmCuAdminProfile object of the PCS port connected to the PME decides, which allows a common profile for all PMEs on that port with individual overrides.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has two halves: one for the port as a whole, one for each line. It also adds a table listing which lines could be joined to which, so a manager can see the options before changing anything.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are a number of managed objects defined in the EFM-CU-MIB module that have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create. Most objects are writeable only when the link is down, but writing to them can have potentially disruptive effects on network operation. Changing efmCuPmeAdminSubType may lead to a potential locking of the link, as peer PMEs of the same subtype cannot exchange handshake messages. Changing efmCuPAFAdminState to enabled may lead to a potential locking of the link if the peer PHY does not support PAF. Changing efmCuPAFDiscoveryCode before the discovery operation may lead to a wrongful discovery, for example when two -O ports are connected to the same multi-PME -R port and both -O ports have the same Discovery register value. Changing PCS or PME configuration parameters may lead to anything from link quality and rate degradation to a complete link initialization failure, since the ability of an EFMCu port to support a particular configuration depends on the copper environment. Activation of a PME can cause a severe degradation of service for another EFMCu PHY whose PMEs may be affected by cross-talk from the newly activated PME, and removal of a PME from an operationally up port that aggregates several PMEs may cause rate degradation. The user of the module must therefore be aware that support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

The readable objects may be considered sensitive in some environments, since collectively they provide information about the performance of network interfaces and can reveal some aspects of their configuration. In particular, since EFMCu can be carried over unshielded twisted pair voice-grade copper in a bundle with other pairs belonging to another operator or customer, it is theoretically possible to eavesdrop on an EFMCu transmission simply by listening to cross-talk from the EFMCu pairs, especially if the parameters of the link are known. It is therefore important to control GET and NOTIFY access to these objects and possibly even to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even if the network itself is secure, there is no control over who on that network may read or change the objects. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy. Deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing these settings can break a working link, so the management access needs to be locked down and encrypted. Reading them can also leak information, because the same cable bundle may carry another customer's lines and the copper picks up crosstalk.
